doc.title: John Lamb interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 16, 2001

title: Playing at Eddie Levine's and meeting Pops Foster
summary: Hearing a lounge group inspires him, and he wins an audition at Eddie Levine's with his five-string Chubby Jackson model bass and meets Pops Foster across the street.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Bass players: lineage, tone and technique

blocks.x: Well I couldn’t go there, no money. But while I was getting my money back, I heard this beautiful bass sound coming out of the room. Somebody was bowing this instrument. I said oh that’s so beautiful, I didn’t realize that a bass could sound like that. And all of this sound was filtering out. I don’t have any idea to this day who that was. But it stayed with me. And while washing these dishes, these pots, there was a group out in the lobby playing. And I looked out there and the guys all had tuxes you know, looking good. And of course I had a little musical background and I said that’s what I’d like to do, you know, play out there in the lounge. I shouldn’t be back here in washing these pots. So it turns out it was Joe Bruno’s father that was playing in that group. And Joe Bruno I met 20 years later, or much later, down in Sarasota. And I also met his son, so I met the father when I was in the kitchen, but not formally but through his music. And then I met the son later on down in Sarasota, and then his other son, his son, who plays bass. So we have three Brunos. But anyway after that little experience I got a job playing in another club, in Eddie Levine’s place on the corner of Mass and Columbus in Boston. And they said hmmm, they gave me an audition and all that. So I played my Ed Safranski solo.
They had a little quartet you know, I mean that’s all I knew. And I’d walk a little time, and I had my Chubby Jackson model five string bass.
Oh you did. I’ll be darned. That’s right he had his own little.

Yeah, he had this five string bass. But you know later on I discovered that Slam Stewart tuned his bass with a high C on top. And I didn’t realize that at the time. And then in that little corner we had the Hi-Hat, we had all the jazz cats come over there. Are you familiar with Boston? Mass Columbus? We had that little corner, we had Wally’s across the street where I met Pops Foster. Pops Foster was 75 about that time and he was claimed to be the first guy to begin plucking the bass. And I said, “Pops, come on over, I want you to catch my act and see how I do on the bass.” So he came out and checked out my sound © Fillius Jazz Archive -9-
